subChunks.title: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, and CHECK
subChunks.hookHtml: Constraints are promises the database enforces automatically — so your application code never has to validate the same rules manually.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
NOT NULL

name TEXT NOT NULL

Rejects any INSERT or UPDATE that would leave this column empty. The most fundamental data quality constraint.

UNIQUE

email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
-- Or at table level (multi-column uniqueness):
UNIQUE (user_id, topic_id)

Prevents duplicate values. Unlike PRIMARY KEY, multiple UNIQUE columns are allowed and UNIQUE columns (unlike PRIMARY KEY) can contain NULL in some engines.

DEFAULT

created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
is_active  BOOLEAN   NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE

Fills in a value automatically when INSERT omits the column.

CHECK

xp     INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (xp >= 0)
score  INTEGER          CHECK (score BETWEEN 0 AND 100)
status TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active','inactive','pending'))

A boolean expression evaluated on every INSERT and UPDATE. If it evaluates to FALSE, the statement is rejected.

Adding constraints after creation

ALTER TABLE apprentices ADD CONSTRAINT chk_xp CHECK (xp >= 0);
ALTER TABLE apprentices ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE (email);

storyBeats.text: 'Without these rules, someone will insert negative XP — and the algorithm will award it.' Cipher stamps the constraints into the ledger's margin.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Each constraint is a promise the archive keeps automatically. NOT NULL says 'this fact always exists.' UNIQUE says 'no two records share this value.' CHECK says 'this value must satisfy this rule.' The more you encode in constraints, the less your application code needs to check.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Constraint analysis

The schema below has three deliberate gaps. Identify what constraint each gap needs and why:

CREATE TABLE apprentices (
  id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  email    TEXT,           -- (1) should be required and unique
  xp       INTEGER,        -- (2) should never be negative
  rank     TEXT            -- (3) should be one of a fixed set
);
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) `email TEXT` — Missing NOT NULL and UNIQUE. Email should be required (NOT NULL) and no two accounts should share an email (UNIQUE): `email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE`.

(2) `xp INTEGER` — Missing NOT NULL and a CHECK constraint: `xp INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (xp >= 0)`. Without the CHECK, a bug in the application could insert negative XP and corrupt the leaderboard.

(3) `rank TEXT` — Missing a CHECK constraint to restrict to valid values: `rank TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (rank IN ('Novice','Apprentice','Adept','Mage','Archmage','Magus'))`. Without it, a typo like 'apprentice' (lowercase) or 'Admin' would be stored silently.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Write a complete CREATE TABLE for quests with proper constraints: id (PK), title (NOT NULL, UNIQUE), xp_reward (NOT NULL, CHECK >= 0), difficulty (NOT NULL, CHECK IN Easy/Medium/Hard/Expert), min_rank (TEXT, nullable).
subChunks.modelAnswer:
CREATE TABLE quests (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title       TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  xp_reward   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (xp_reward >= 0),
  difficulty  TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (difficulty IN ('Easy','Medium','Hard','Expert')),
  min_rank    TEXT
);
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a CHECK constraint does, give two examples where it prevents a real bug, and explain how it differs from application-level validation.

questions.prompt: What does a UNIQUE constraint guarantee?
options: No two rows in the table have the same value in that column (or combination of columns)
The column has a non-NULL value in every row
The column values are in sorted order
The column values are always positive
questions.answer: No two rows in the table have the same value in that column (or combination of columns)
questions.explanation: UNIQUE enforces that every value in the column (or column combination) is distinct. It differs from PRIMARY KEY in that multiple UNIQUE constraints are allowed and UNIQUE columns may contain NULL.

questions.prompt: A row is inserted with `xp = -50` into a column defined as `xp INTEGER CHECK (xp >= 0)`. What happens?
options: The INSERT is rejected — the CHECK constraint is violated
The value is silently clamped to 0
The INSERT succeeds — CHECK is advisory only
questions.answer: The INSERT is rejected — the CHECK constraint is violated
questions.explanation: CHECK constraints are enforced at INSERT and UPDATE time. If the expression evaluates to FALSE, the statement is rejected with a constraint violation error. There is no clamping or coercion.

questions.prompt: What does `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` do for a `created_at` column?
options: Automatically sets created_at to the current date and time when a row is inserted and the column is not explicitly provided
Sets created_at to the time the table was created
questions.answer: Automatically sets created_at to the current date and time when a row is inserted and the column is not explicitly provided
questions.explanation: DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP fills in the current timestamp at INSERT time when the column is omitted. It does not update automatically on UPDATE — that requires a trigger or explicit UPDATE.

questions.prompt: Why are database constraints better than application-level validation for data integrity?
options: Constraints enforce rules at the database level regardless of which application, API, or admin tool inserts the data
Constraints are faster to write than application code
Constraints can express more complex logic than application code
Application validation is deprecated in modern databases
questions.answer: Constraints enforce rules at the database level regardless of which application, API, or admin tool inserts the data
questions.explanation: Application validation can be bypassed — by a different microservice, a direct SQL client, a migration script, or a bug. Database constraints are the last line of defence that no path around the database can circumvent.
